notes.front: How does SP 800-61r3 define a cybersecurity incident?
notes.back: An occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardises information or a system's confidentiality, integrity or availability without lawful authority, or violates law or security policy.
notes.explanation: The definition covers imminent harm as well as actual harm, and breaches of policies and acceptable use as well as attacks on the CIA triad.
notes.example: Like a break-in at a shop: it counts whether the thief got away with stock or was caught forcing the lock.
notes.evidence: A cybersecurity incident (or simply incident) is …an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes, without lawful authority, the integrity, confidentiality, or availability of information or an information system; or constitutes a violation or imminent threat of violation of law, security policies, security procedures, or acceptable use policies.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: In SP 800-61r3, what does incident management involve?
notes.back: Overseeing responses to all incidents and shifting priorities and resources as needed.
notes.explanation: SP 800-61r3 calls evaluating an incident's overall risk and prioritising it perhaps the most critical decision points in incident response.
notes.example: Like a hospital's duty manager during a busy night, moving doctors between wards as cases arrive, rather than treating any one patient.
notes.evidence: N1: Incident management involves overseeing responses to all incidents and shifting priorities and resources as needed. Evaluating the overall risk from an incident and applying the appropriate prioritization are perhaps the most critical decision points in the incident response process.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Table 3 Respond (RS.MA Incident Management), PDF p. 34

notes.front: In SP 800-61r3, what do lessons learned from incident response activities and root cause analysis help improve?
notes.back: Cybersecurity risk management.
notes.explanation: Lessons learned are what an organisation takes from its incident response work and from finding root causes, fed back into how it manages risk.
notes.example: Like a football team rewatching a lost match and changing how it trains, not just replaying the same tactics.
notes.evidence: Lessons learned from incident response activities and root cause analysis help improve cybersecurity risk management
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: What is a firewall, according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: A device or program that controls the flow of network traffic between networks or hosts with differing security postures.
notes.explanation: The definition is about differing security postures, not location: most firewalls were once at network perimeters, but that is not what makes them firewalls.
notes.example: Like a border checkpoint between two countries with different rules, deciding which lorries may cross.
notes.evidence: Firewalls are devices or programs that control the flow of network traffic between networks or hosts that employ differing security postures. At one time, most firewalls were deployed at network perimeters.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Executive Summary, PDF p. 7

notes.front: What is the distinguishing feature of a next-generation firewall (NGFW), according to SP 800-215?
notes.back: Application data awareness: it looks at layer 7, the application level, as well as layers 3 and 4.
notes.explanation: SP 800-215 says its capabilities extend beyond packet filtering and stateful inspection.
notes.example: Like a customs officer who opens the parcels, not one who only reads the address labels.
notes.evidence: Next-generation firewall (NGFW): The distinguishing feature of NGFW is application data awareness. It can look at data not only at layers 3 and 4 of an Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) stack but also at layer 7 – the application level. Its capabilities extend beyond packet filtering and stateful inspection.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, Section 3 Network security, PDF p. 19

notes.front: What is a web application firewall (WAF), according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: A specialised application firewall that sits in front of a web server and can detect many exploits of the web protocol.
notes.explanation: It is a specialised kind of application firewall, dedicated to the web server behind it.
notes.example: Like a bouncer posted at one particular club's door, checking only people heading into that club.
notes.evidence: Many of these exploits can be detected by specialized application firewalls called web application firewalls that reside in front of the web server.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.9 Web Application Firewalls, PDF p. 19

notes.front: In SP 800-53's least functionality control, what does allowlisting (authorised software, allow-by-exception) require?
notes.back: Identifying the software authorised to run, and applying a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy so only that software executes.
notes.explanation: Anything not on the list of authorised programs is denied by default.
notes.example: Like a private party with a guest list: anyone whose name is not on it is turned away.
notes.evidence: AUTHORIZED SOFTWARE — ALLOW-BY-EXCEPTION (a) Identify [Assignment: organization-defined software programs authorized to execute on the system]; (b) Employ a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy to allow the execution of authorized software programs on the system;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, CM-7(5) Authorized Software — Allow-by-Exception, PDF p. 133

notes.front: In SP 800-53's least functionality control, what does denylisting (unauthorised software, deny-by-exception) require?
notes.back: Identifying the software not authorised to run, and applying an allow-all, deny-by-exception policy to block it.
notes.explanation: Everything not on the list of unauthorised programs is allowed by default.
notes.example: Like a pub's list of barred customers: everyone else walks straight in.
notes.evidence: UNAUTHORIZED SOFTWARE — DENY-BY-EXCEPTION (a) Identify [Assignment: organization-defined software programs not authorized to execute on the system]; (b) Employ an allow-all, deny-by-exception policy to prohibit the execution of unauthorized software programs on the system;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, CM-7(4) Unauthorized Software — Deny-by-Exception, PDF p. 133

notes.front: What is a sandbox, in the sandboxing security model SP 800-83 describes?
notes.back: A controlled environment that restricts what operations applications can perform and isolates them from other applications on the same host.
notes.explanation: Only permitted operations can run inside it, and what runs there is kept apart from the host's other applications.
notes.example: Like a children's play pen: what happens inside stays inside, and the toys cannot reach the kitchen.
notes.evidence: Sandboxing refers to a security model where applications are run within a sandbox—a controlled environment that restricts what operations the applications can perform and that isolates them from other applications running on the same host.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1, Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops, Section 3.5.2 Sandboxing, PDF p. 26

notes.front: What is a honeypot, according to SP 800-94?
notes.back: A host with no authorised users besides its administrators, because it serves no business function; all activity aimed at it is considered suspicious.
notes.explanation: Because nobody has a legitimate reason to touch it, any activity at all stands out.
notes.example: Like a fake parcel left on a doorstep with a tracker inside: nobody should pick it up, so whoever does is worth watching.
notes.evidence: Honeypots are hosts that have no authorized users other than the honeypot administrators because they serve no business function; all activity directed at them is considered suspicious.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), Section 8.3.4 Honeypots, PDF p. 91

notes.front: In SP 800-53, what kind of control is a honeynet, and what is it established to do?
notes.back: A decoy, like a honeypot or deception net: established to attract adversaries and deflect attacks away from operational systems.
notes.explanation: SP 800-53 groups honeypots, honeynets and deception nets together as decoys that protect the systems supporting the organisation's mission.
notes.example: Like a museum's dummy display room, laid out to draw thieves away from the real collection.
notes.evidence: Decoys (i.e., honeypots, honeynets, or deception nets) are established to attract adversaries and deflect attacks away from the operational systems that support organizational mission and business functions.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-26 Decoys, PDF p. 343

notes.front: What is malware, according to SP 800-83?
notes.back: A program covertly inserted into another program to destroy data, run destructive or intrusive programs, or otherwise compromise confidentiality, integrity or availability.
notes.explanation: SP 800-83 also calls it malicious code; the target can be the victim's data, applications or operating system.
notes.example: Like a saboteur hidden in a delivery crate, slipped into the warehouse along with the legitimate goods.
notes.evidence: Malware, also known as malicious code, refers to a program that is covertly inserted into another program with the intent to destroy data, run destructive or intrusive programs, or otherwise compromise the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the victim’s data, applications, or operating system.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1, Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: Which two kinds of software does SP 800-94 group as anti-malware technologies?
notes.back: Antivirus software and antispyware software.
notes.explanation: SP 800-94 treats anti-malware as a technology that complements intrusion detection and prevention systems.
notes.example: Like a building's pest control contract that covers both mice and insects.
notes.evidence: This section discusses common types of complementary technologies: network forensic analysis tools, anti-malware technologies (antivirus software and antispyware software), firewalls and routers, and honeypots.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), Section 8.3 Other technologies, PDF p. 88

notes.front: In SP 800-61r3's model, lessons learned from which Functions are fed into the Improvement category?
notes.back: From performing all activities in all Functions; they are then used to inform all of the Functions.
notes.explanation: The lessons are analysed and prioritised before they inform the Functions, so organisations can learn at any time.
notes.evidence: Lessons learned from performing all activities in all Functions are fed into Improvement, and those lessons are analyzed, prioritized, and used to inform all of the Functions.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 2.1 Incident Response Life Cycle Model, PDF p. 13

notes.front: When should lessons learned during incident response often be shared, according to SP 800-61r3?
notes.back: As soon as they are identified, not delayed until after recovery concludes.
notes.explanation: SP 800-61r3 now treats incident response as part of risk management, where continuous improvement is increasingly necessary to keep up with modern threats.
notes.evidence: The lessons learned during incident response should often be shared as soon as they are identified, not delayed until after recovery concludes. Continuous improvement is increasingly necessary for all facets of cybersecurity risk management in order to keep up with modern threats.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 2.1 Incident Response Life Cycle Model, PDF p. 12

notes.front: What changes in incidents does SP 800-61r3 cite for moving away from its earlier circular incident response life cycle?
notes.back: Incidents now occur frequently and cause far more damage, and recovery often takes weeks or months.
notes.explanation: SP 800-61r3 now treats incident response as a critical part of risk management, integrated across the organisation's operations.
notes.evidence: Today, incidents occur frequently and cause far more damage. Recovering from them often takes weeks or months due to their breadth, complexity, and dynamic nature. Incident response is now considered a critical part of cybersecurity risk management that should be integrated across organizational operations.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 2.1 Incident Response Life Cycle Model, PDF p. 12

notes.front: In SP 800-61r3's model, which three CSF 2.0 Functions make up incident response itself?
notes.back: Detect, Respond and Recover.
notes.explanation: They form the top level of the model's figure; Govern, Identify and Protect sit below as broader risk management that supports incident response.
notes.evidence: The bottom level reflects that the preparation activities of Govern, Identify, and Protect are not part of the incident response itself. Rather, they are much broader cybersecurity risk management activities that also support incident response. Incident response is shown in the top level of the figure: Detect, Respond, and Recover.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 2.1 Incident Response Life Cycle Model, PDF p. 13

notes.front: How do Govern, Identify and Protect help incident response in SP 800-61r3's model?
notes.back: They help prevent some incidents, prepare to handle those that occur, reduce their impact, and improve practices based on lessons learned.
notes.explanation: SP 800-61r3 says all six CSF 2.0 Functions have vital roles in incident response.
notes.evidence: All six Functions have vital roles in incident response. Govern, Identify, and Protect help organizations prevent some incidents, prepare to handle incidents that do occur, reduce the impact of those incidents, and improve incident response and cybersecurity risk management practices based on lessons learned.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 2.1 Incident Response Life Cycle Model, PDF p. 13

notes.front: In SP 800-61r3's Table 1, which CSF 2.0 Functions correspond to the old 'preparation' phase?
notes.back: Govern, Identify (all categories) and Protect.
notes.explanation: Table 1 maps each phase of the previous SP 800-61 life cycle to the CSF 2.0 Functions the new model uses.
notes.evidence: Table 1 maps the previous SP 800-61 incident response life cycle model’s phases to the corresponding CSF 2.0 Functions used in this document. Table 1. Previous incident response life cycle model’s phases and corresponding CSF 2.0 Functions Previous Incident Response Life Cycle Model Phase CSF 2.0 Functions Govern Preparation Identify (all Categories) Protect
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 2.1, Table 1, PDF p. 14

notes.front: SP 800-53's incident handling control requires a capability that includes preparation, detection and analysis, {{c1::containment, eradication}}, and recovery.
notes.explanation: The capability must also be consistent with the organisation's incident response plan.
notes.evidence: Implement an incident handling capability for incidents that is consistent with the incident response plan and includes preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, IR-4 Incident Handling, PDF p. 179

notes.front: Under SP 800-53's incident handling control, with which other activities must incident handling be coordinated?
notes.back: Contingency planning activities.
notes.explanation: The same control also asks that handling be comparable and predictable across the organisation.
notes.evidence: b. Coordinate incident handling activities with contingency planning activities; c. Incorporate lessons learned from ongoing incident handling activities into incident response procedures, training, and testing, and implement the resulting changes accordingly; and d. Ensure the rigor, intensity, scope, and results of incident handling activities are comparable and predictable across the organization.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, IR-4 Incident Handling, PDF p. 179

notes.front: Under SP 800-53's incident reporting control, what must personnel report, to whom, and when?
notes.back: Suspected incidents, to the organisational incident response capability, within an organisation-defined time period.
notes.explanation: The control's second part has the organisation report incident information on to authorities it defines.
notes.evidence: Require personnel to report suspected incidents to the organizational incident response capability within [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and b. Report incident information to [Assignment: organization-defined authorities].
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, IR-6 Incident Reporting, PDF p. 184

notes.front: What are two things incident information can inform, according to the discussion of SP 800-53's incident reporting control?
notes.back: Any two of: risk assessments, control effectiveness assessments, security requirements for acquisitions, selection criteria for technology products.
notes.explanation: Reporting is not only a duty to authorities; the reports also feed the organisation's own risk and acquisition decisions.
notes.evidence: Incident information can inform risk assessments, control effectiveness assessments, security requirements for acquisitions, and selection criteria for technology products.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, IR-6 Incident Reporting, PDF p. 184

notes.front: SP 800-61r3 says an organisation's incident handlers may be on staff, on contract or available when needed. What is its example of 'on contract'?
notes.back: Outsourcing a security operations centre to a managed security services provider, or using a cloud provider's incident response team.
notes.explanation: Security services provided by a third party are one of the ways SP 800-61r3 expects incident handling to be staffed.
notes.evidence: On contract (e.g., outsourcing a security operations center [SOC] to a managed security services provider [MSSP] or leveraging a cloud service provider’s incident response team when an incident occurs within that provider’s cloud)
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 2.2 Incident Response Roles and Responsibilities, PDF p. 15

notes.front: Why do network designers now often put firewall functionality at places other than the network perimeter, according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: Perimeter firewalls cannot recognise every form of attack, and attacks between internal hosts often never pass through them.
notes.explanation: Firewalls inside the network add a further layer of security behind the perimeter.
notes.evidence: it could not recognize all instances and forms of attack, and attacks sent from one internal host to another often do not pass through network firewalls. Because of these and other factors, network designers now often include firewall functionality at places other than the network perimeter to provide an additional layer of security
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Executive Summary, PDF p. 7

notes.front: SP 800-41 says threats have moved to the application layer, reducing firewalls' general effectiveness. Why are firewalls still needed?
notes.back: To stop the significant threats that continue to work at lower layers of network traffic.
notes.explanation: The shift upward weakened firewalls against application-layer threats without removing the lower-layer ones.
notes.evidence: Threats have gradually moved from being most prevalent in lower layers of network traffic to the application layer, which has reduced the general effectiveness of firewalls in stopping threats carried through network communications. However, firewalls are still needed to stop the significant threats that continue to work at lower layers of network traffic.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Executive Summary, PDF p. 7

notes.front: SP 800-41 calls the packet filter the most basic firewall feature. What do firewalls that are only packet filters not do?
notes.back: Keep track of the state of each flow of traffic; they are also known as stateless inspection firewalls.
notes.explanation: Older packet-filter-only firewalls were essentially routing devices that provided access control for host addresses and communication sessions.
notes.evidence: The most basic feature of a firewall is the packet filter. Older firewalls that were only packet filters were essentially routing devices that provided access control functionality for host addresses and communication sessions. These devices, also known as stateless inspection firewalls, do not keep track of the state of each flow of traffic
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.1 Packet Filtering, PDF p. 12

notes.front: How does stateful inspection improve on packet filtering, according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: It tracks the state of connections and blocks packets that deviate from the expected state.
notes.explanation: It does this with greater awareness of the transport layer.
notes.evidence: Stateful inspection improves on the functions of packet filters by tracking the state of connections and blocking packets that deviate from the expected state. This is accomplished by incorporating greater awareness of the transport layer.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.2 Stateful Inspection, PDF p. 14

notes.front: What capability do application firewalls add to standard stateful inspection, according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: Stateful protocol analysis (called deep packet inspection by some vendors): comparing application-layer activity with profiles of benign protocol activity.
notes.explanation: It adds basic intrusion detection technology, so the firewall can allow or deny access based on how an application is running over the network.
notes.evidence: Stateful protocol analysis improves upon standard stateful inspection by adding basic intrusion detection technology—an inspection engine that analyzes protocols at the application layer to compare vendor-developed profiles of benign protocol activity against observed events to identify deviations. This allows a firewall to allow or deny access based on how an application is running over the network.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.3 Application Firewalls, PDF p. 15

notes.front: How does an application-proxy gateway handle a connection between two hosts, according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: It never allows a direct connection: each attempt becomes two connections, client to proxy and proxy to destination.
notes.explanation: The proxy server sits in the middle: the client and the true destination each connect only to it.
notes.evidence: Each successful connection attempt actually results in the creation of two separate connections—one between the client and the proxy server, and another between the proxy server and the true destination.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.4 Application-Proxy Gateways, PDF p. 16

notes.front: Where does a host-based or personal firewall run, and whose traffic does it control, according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: It is software on the host it protects, monitoring and controlling incoming and outgoing traffic for that single host.
notes.explanation: Being on the host, it can give more granular protection than a network firewall to meet that host's needs.
notes.evidence: These firewalls are software-based, residing on the hosts they are protecting—each monitors and controls the incoming and outgoing network traffic for a single host. They can provide more granular protection than network firewalls to meet the needs of specific hosts.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.2.1 Host-Based Firewalls and Personal Firewalls, PDF p. 20

notes.front: Why are web application firewalls often considered very different from traditional firewalls, according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: Because they are put in front of web servers to prevent attacks on the server.
notes.explanation: SP 800-41 ties the difference to where they sit and what they protect: web servers.
notes.evidence: Because they are put in front of web servers to prevent attacks on the server, they are often considered to be very different than traditional firewalls.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.9 Web Application Firewalls, PDF p. 19

notes.front: How can sandboxing help against malware, according to SP 800-83?
notes.back: By limiting the operations available, it can stop some or all of the malware's malicious actions, preventing success or reducing damage.
notes.explanation: The effect is hedged: sandboxing could prevent the malware succeeding, or only reduce the damage it causes.
notes.evidence: By limiting the operations available, it can prevent malware from performing some or all of the malicious actions it is attempting to execute; this could prevent the malware from succeeding or reduce the damage it causes.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1, Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops, Section 3.5.2 Sandboxing, PDF p. 26

notes.front: What does SP 800-53 call a capability for opening email attachments and running suspicious applications in an isolated environment or virtualised sandbox?
notes.back: A detonation chamber, also known as a dynamic execution environment.
notes.explanation: The isolation lets the organisation examine untrusted content, including web address requests, safely.
notes.evidence: Detonation chambers, also known as dynamic execution environments, allow organizations to open email attachments, execute untrusted or suspicious applications, and execute Universal Resource Locator requests in the safety of an isolated environment or a virtualized sandbox.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-44 Detonation Chambers, PDF p. 355

notes.front: What do honeypots give administrators, and what are they relative to intrusion detection and prevention systems, per SP 800-94?
notes.back: Data on new attack trends and tools, especially malware; they supplement, not replace, controls such as intrusion detection and prevention systems.
notes.explanation: Attackers scan and attack honeypots, and that activity is what yields the data.
notes.evidence: Attackers will scan and attack honeypots, giving administrators data on new trends and attack tools, particularly malware. However, honeypots are a supplement to, not a replacement for, other security controls such as intrusion detection and prevention systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), Section 8.3.4 Honeypots, PDF p. 91

notes.front: What does SP 800-53 say using decoys such as honeypots and honeynets requires?
notes.back: Supporting isolation measures, so any deflected malicious code does not infect organisational systems.
notes.explanation: The isolation keeps malicious code deflected to the decoy away from organisational systems.
notes.evidence: Use of decoys requires some supporting isolation measures to ensure that any deflected malicious code does not infect organizational systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-26 Decoys, PDF p. 343

notes.front: What does SP 800-83 call malware, in terms of external threats to most hosts?
notes.back: The most common external threat to most hosts.
notes.explanation: SP 800-83 says it causes widespread damage and disruption and needs extensive recovery efforts in most organisations.
notes.evidence: Malware is the most common external threat to most hosts, causing widespread damage and disruption and necessitating extensive recovery efforts within most organizations.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1, Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: Which malware threat mitigation technical control does SP 800-83 call the most commonly used, and where should it be deployed?
notes.back: Antivirus software, on all hosts for which satisfactory antivirus software is available.
notes.explanation: The recommendation is hedged: it applies where satisfactory antivirus software exists for the host.
notes.evidence: The most commonly used malware threat mitigation technical control is antivirus software; organizations should deploy antivirus software on all hosts for which satisfactory antivirus software is available.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1, Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops, Executive Summary, PDF p. 9

notes.front: Besides antivirus software, what are two technical controls SP 800-83 finds helpful for malware threat mitigation?
notes.back: Any two of: intrusion prevention systems, firewalls, content filtering and inspection, application allowlisting.
notes.explanation: SP 800-83 calls the last of these application whitelisting.
notes.evidence: Additional technical controls that are helpful for malware threat mitigation include intrusion prevention systems, firewalls, content filtering and inspection, and application whitelisting.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1, Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops, Executive Summary, PDF p. 9

notes.front: Overnight, a contractor's account copies a customer file it has no right to read. Nothing has left the network yet. Under SP 800-61r3's definition, is this an incident?
notes.back: Yes: it actually jeopardises confidentiality without lawful authority.
notes.choices:
A) No: no data has left the network yet
B) Yes: it actually jeopardises confidentiality without lawful authority
C) Only once a court finds that a law was broken
notes.choicesExplained: A: the definition covers occurrences that jeopardise confidentiality, actually or imminently, not only completed leaks. C: a violation of security policy is enough; no court ruling is needed.
notes.explanation: Unauthorised access to the file already jeopardises its confidentiality, which meets the first limb of the definition.
notes.evidence: an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes, without lawful authority, the integrity, confidentiality, or availability of information or an information system; or constitutes a violation or imminent threat of violation of law, security policies, security procedures, or acceptable use policies.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: Responders are cutting infected laptops off the network to stop an outbreak spreading. Which CSF 2.0 Function in SP 800-61r3's model covers this?
notes.back: Respond.
notes.choices:
A) Protect
B) Respond
C) Recover
notes.choicesExplained: A: Protect is preparation that sits outside incident response itself. C: Recover restores assets and operations affected by the incident; cutting machines off is not restoring them.
notes.explanation: Respond is where actions are taken on a detected incident, and SP 800-61r3 names containing incidents among the jobs of Detect, Respond and Recover.
notes.evidence: Respond (RS): Actions regarding a detected cybersecurity incident are taken. • Recover (RC): Assets and operations affected by a cybersecurity incident are restored.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 2.1 Incident Response Life Cycle Model, PDF p. 13

notes.front: Midway through a month-long recovery, an analyst finds that a detection rule has been missing for a year. When does SP 800-61r3 suggest sharing this lesson?
notes.back: Now, as soon as it is identified.
notes.choices:
A) Now, as soon as it is identified
B) In the post-incident review after recovery ends
C) At the next annual plan review
notes.choicesExplained: B: SP 800-61r3 says lessons should often not be delayed until after recovery concludes. C: waiting for an annual review delays it even further.
notes.explanation: SP 800-61r3 says lessons learned during incident response should often be shared as soon as they are identified.
notes.evidence: The lessons learned during incident response should often be shared as soon as they are identified, not delayed until after recovery concludes.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Section 2.1 Incident Response Life Cycle Model, PDF p. 12

notes.front: After a phishing incident, the team finds its playbook had no step for resetting stolen tokens. Under SP 800-53's incident handling control, what should follow?
notes.back: Fold the lesson into incident response procedures, training and testing, and implement the changes.
notes.choices:
A) Record it in the incident ticket and close it
B) Fold the lesson into incident response procedures, training and testing, and implement the changes
C) Report it to external authorities as a new incident
notes.choicesExplained: A: recording alone does not change procedures, training or testing. C: the gap is a lesson about handling, not a new incident to report.
notes.explanation: The incident handling control asks for lessons learned from ongoing handling to be incorporated and the resulting changes implemented.
notes.evidence: Incorporate lessons learned from ongoing incident handling activities into incident response procedures, training, and testing, and implement the resulting changes accordingly;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, IR-4 Incident Handling, PDF p. 179

notes.front: An engineer notices an administrator login from an unknown country at 3 a.m. and plans to mention it in next month's status report. What does SP 800-53's incident reporting control expect?
notes.back: Report the suspected incident to the incident response capability within the organisation-defined time.
notes.choices:
A) Wait until the login is confirmed as malicious
B) Report the suspected incident to the incident response capability within the organisation-defined time
C) Report it straight to outside authorities only
notes.choicesExplained: A: the control covers suspected incidents, not only confirmed ones. C: personnel report to the organisation's own incident response capability; the organisation reports onward to its defined authorities.
notes.explanation: The control is about suspected incidents and a time limit the organisation sets, so a monthly report may be too late.
notes.evidence: Require personnel to report suspected incidents to the organizational incident response capability within [Assignment: organization-defined time period];
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, IR-6 Incident Reporting, PDF p. 184

notes.front: An attacker on one internal server moves to another server on the same subnet, and the perimeter firewall logs nothing. What does SP 800-41 suggest to close this gap?
notes.back: Host-based firewalls on the servers, allowing only necessary traffic.
notes.choices:
A) A stricter rule set on the perimeter firewall
B) Host-based firewalls on the servers, allowing only necessary traffic
C) Removing the perimeter firewall
notes.choicesExplained: A: traffic between internal hosts does not pass through the perimeter firewall, so its rules never apply. C: SP 800-41 still sees a role for perimeter firewalls against lower-layer threats.
notes.explanation: A host-based firewall protects against malicious activity from all hosts, including those on the same subnet.
notes.evidence: Configuring a hostbased firewall to allow only necessary traffic to the server provides protection against malicious activity from all hosts, including those on the same subnet or on other internal subnets not separated by a network firewall.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.2.1 Host-Based Firewalls and Personal Firewalls, PDF p. 20

notes.front: A design review says outside servers must never connect directly to internal clients, and internal addresses must stay hidden. Which firewall technology fits best?
notes.back: An application-proxy gateway.
notes.choices:
A) A stateless packet filter
B) A stateful inspection firewall
C) An application-proxy gateway
notes.choicesExplained: A: a packet filter passes permitted packets straight through between hosts. B: stateful inspection tracks connections but still lets the two hosts connect to each other.
notes.explanation: The proxy splits each connection in two, so outside hosts only ever talk to the proxy agent.
notes.evidence: These firewalls contain a proxy agent that acts as an intermediary between two hosts that wish to communicate with each other, and never allows a direct connection between them.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.4 Application-Proxy Gateways, PDF p. 16

notes.front: An online bookshop keeps seeing attacks crafted against its web server's pages. Which control, placed in front of the server, is designed for this?
notes.back: A web application firewall.
notes.choices:
A) A web application firewall
B) A personal firewall on each customer's laptop
C) A honeypot
notes.choicesExplained: B: personal firewalls protect the customer's own computer, not the shop's server. C: a honeypot attracts attackers to a decoy but does not screen traffic to the real server.
notes.explanation: A WAF resides in front of the web server to detect exploits aimed at it.
notes.evidence: Many of these exploits can be detected by specialized application firewalls called web application firewalls that reside in front of the web server.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.9 Web Application Firewalls, PDF p. 19

notes.front: A hospital's waiting-room kiosk must run one approved browser and nothing else. Which approach from SP 800-53's least functionality control fits?
notes.back: Allowlisting: deny all, permit by exception.
notes.choices:
A) Denylisting: allow all, deny by exception
B) Allowlisting: deny all, permit by exception
C) Antivirus scanning only
notes.choicesExplained: A: a denylist lets any program run unless it is listed, so unknown programs could still run. C: antivirus looks for malware but does not limit the kiosk to one program.
notes.explanation: Only programs identified as authorised may execute, which matches a single approved browser.
notes.evidence: Employ a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy to allow the execution of authorized software programs on the system;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, CM-7(5) Authorized Software — Allow-by-Exception, PDF p. 133

notes.front: An analyst receives an invoice attachment she suspects is booby-trapped and wants to see what it does. What is the safest way, per SP 800-53?
notes.back: Open it in a detonation chamber: an isolated environment or virtualised sandbox.
notes.choices:
A) Open it on her own workstation with antivirus running
B) Open it in a detonation chamber: an isolated environment or virtualised sandbox
C) Forward it to colleagues to check
notes.choicesExplained: A: her workstation is not isolated, so anything the file does happens there. C: forwarding spreads the suspect file to more users.
notes.explanation: Detonation chambers exist to open attachments and run suspicious code safely in isolation.
notes.evidence: allow organizations to open email attachments, execute untrusted or suspicious applications, and execute Universal Resource Locator requests in the safety of an isolated environment or a virtualized sandbox.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-44 Detonation Chambers, PDF p. 355

notes.front: A server that exists only as a honeypot records a login attempt from a finance laptop. How should the team treat it?
notes.back: As suspicious, because nobody has a business reason to touch the honeypot.
notes.choices:
A) As normal traffic, since it came from inside
B) As suspicious, because nobody has a business reason to touch the honeypot
C) As a false positive to be tuned out
notes.choicesExplained: A: an internal source does not make it legitimate; the honeypot has no authorised users besides its administrators. C: with no business function, there is no normal activity to mistake it for.
notes.explanation: All activity directed at a honeypot is considered suspicious, whatever its source.
notes.evidence: Honeypots are hosts that have no authorized users other than the honeypot administrators because they serve no business function; all activity directed at them is considered suspicious.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), Section 8.3.4 Honeypots, PDF p. 91

notes.front: A spreadsheet arrives with hidden code that quietly deletes files when the sheet is opened. How does SP 800-83 classify this?
notes.back: Malware: a program covertly inserted into another with intent to destroy data.
notes.choices:
A) Malware: a program covertly inserted into another with intent to destroy data
B) A software bug with no malicious intent
C) A honeypot
notes.choicesExplained: B: the code was hidden and deletes files on purpose, so there is intent. C: a honeypot is a decoy host, not code inside a document.
notes.explanation: Covert insertion plus intent to destroy data matches SP 800-83's definition of malware.
notes.evidence: Malware, also known as malicious code, refers to a program that is covertly inserted into another program with the intent to destroy data
notes.source: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1, Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: An audit finds antivirus on office desktops but not on file servers, although satisfactory antivirus exists for them. What does SP 800-83 recommend?
notes.back: Deploy antivirus software on the servers too: on all hosts for which satisfactory antivirus is available.
notes.choices:
A) Leave the servers, since desktops are where users open files
B) Deploy antivirus software on the servers too: on all hosts for which satisfactory antivirus is available
C) Replace antivirus with a honeypot
notes.choicesExplained: A: the recommendation covers all hosts with satisfactory antivirus, not only desktops. C: honeypots supplement other controls and do not scan hosts for malware.
notes.explanation: The only exception SP 800-83 allows is a host for which no satisfactory antivirus software is available.
notes.evidence: organizations should deploy antivirus software on all hosts for which satisfactory antivirus software is available.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1, Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops, Executive Summary, PDF p. 9

notes.front: SP 800-41 compares deny by default with permitting all traffic not explicitly forbidden. Which is more secure, and why?
notes.back: Deny by default, because hosts, networks, protocols and applications keep changing.
notes.explanation: The same allow-versus-deny choice underlies allowlisting and denylisting of software.
notes.evidence: Because of the dynamic nature of hosts, networks, protocols, and applications, deny by default is a more secure approach than permitting all traffic that is not explicitly forbidden.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 4 Firewall Policy, PDF p. 28

notes.front: What does a stateful inspection firewall keep that a packet filter does not?
notes.back: A state table tracking each connection.
notes.explanation: Both intercept packets at the network layer and check them against the rule set; only stateful inspection also tracks connections.
notes.evidence: As with packet filtering, stateful inspection intercepts packets at the network layer and inspects them to see if they are permitted by an existing firewall rule, but unlike packet filtering, stateful inspection keeps track of each connection in a state table.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.2 Stateful Inspection, PDF p. 14

notes.front: Why can an application-proxy gateway offer higher security than an application firewall for some applications, according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: It prevents direct connections between the two hosts and inspects traffic content for policy violations.
notes.explanation: SP 800-41 calls the two technologies quite different, even though both work at the application layer.
notes.evidence: Application-proxy gateways are quite different than application firewalls. First, an application-proxy gateway can offer a higher level of security for some applications because it prevents direct connections between two hosts and it inspects traffic content to identify policy violations.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, Section 2.1.4 Application-Proxy Gateways, PDF p. 16
